metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Pegram v. Herdrich

Opinion filed: 2000-06-12

Docket No.: 98-1949

Citations:
• 147 L. Ed. 2d 164
• 120 S. Ct. 2143
• 530 U.S. 211
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 3964

Case holding summaries:
• explaining that the Employee Retirement Income Security Act altered the common law of trusts to permit certain actions that would otherwise violate the trustee’s fiduciary duties
• “[W]e may use [a party’s] brief to clarify allegations in her complaint whose meaning is unclear.” (citing CHARLES ALLEN WRIGHT & ARTHUR R. MILLER, FEDERAL PRACTICE AND PROCEDURE § 1364 (1990))
• stating that plaintiff's amended complaint "alleged ERISA violations, over which the federal courts have jurisdiction, and we therefore have jurisdiction regardless of the correctness of the removal"
• "The most fundamental duty owed by the trustee to the beneficiaries of the trust is the duty of loyalty.... It is the duty of a trustee to administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries." (internal quotation marks omitted)
• ERISA defines party as fiduciary "only `to the extent' that he acts in such a capacity in relation to a plan"
• stating that plaintiff’s amended complaint “alleged ERISA violations, over which the federal courts have jurisdiction, and we therefore have jurisdiction regardless of the correctness of the removal”
• holding that, “[i]n every case charging breach of ERISA fiduciary duty, . . . the threshold question is 5 Case: 14-20358 Document: 00513037434 Page: 6 Date Filed: 05/11/2015 No. 14-20358 . . . whether that person was acting as a fiduciary . . . when taking the action subject to complaint”
• “Rules governing collection of premiums, definition of benefits, submission of claims, and resolution of disagreements over entitlement to services are the sorts of provisions that constitute a plan.”
• recognizing that, factually, a trustee under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 can both act as ERISA fiduciary and act on behalf of the employer
• explaining that “persons who provide services to an ERISA plan” may operate with a conflict of interest, so long as they comply with fiduciary duties while acting in fiduciary capacity
• explaining that the Employee Retirement Income Security Act altered the common law of trusts to permit certain actions that would otherwise violate the trustee’s fiduciary duties
• court's determination whether mixed eligibility decisions by HMO physicians conferred fiduciary status under ERISA depended on analysis of fact and law
• holding that there was “jurisdiction regardless of the correctness of the removal” because the “amended complaint alleged ERISA violations, over which the federal courts have jurisdiction”
• explaining an ERISA trustee "may wear different hats" and is not necessarily acting as a fiduciary at all times
• “Judicial estoppel generally prevents a party from prevailing in one phase of a case on an argument and then relying on a contradictory argument to prevail in another phase.”
• "[T]he threshold question is not whether the actions of some person employed to provide services under a plan adversely affected a plan beneficiary's interest, but whether that person was acting as a fiduciary (that is, was performing a fiduciary function
• holding that as to Title I fiduciaries, "ERISA ... require[s] ... that the fiduciary with two hats wear only one at a time, and wear the fiduciary hat when making fiduciary decisions"
• no preemption of state law under ERISA "without clear manifestation of congressional purpose"
• "'The most fundamental duty owed by the trustee to the beneficiaries of the trust is the duty of loyalty. . . . It is the duty of a trustee to administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries.'" (quoting 2A A. Scott & W. Fratcher, Trusts 170, at 311 (4th ed. 1987))
• rejecting claims attacking financial incentives behind HMO structure, in light of congr essional policy of promoting HMOs
• "ERISA was not enacted... in order to federalize malpractice litigation...."
• holding that challenges to mixed eligibility and treatment decisions made by an HMO are not preempted by ERISA
• “[W]e may use [a party’s] brief to clarify allegations in her complaint whose meaning is unclear.” (citations omitted)
• ERISA defines party as fiduciary "only `to the extent' that he acts in such a capacity in relation to a plan"
• concluding that "when employers contract with an HMO to provide benefits to employees subject to ERISA, the provisions of documents that set up the HMO are not, as such, an ERISA plan"
• holding that treatment decisions of HMOs are not preempted by ERISA
• “[W]e may use [the parties’] brief to clarify allegations in [their] complaint whose meaning is unclear.” (citing Charles Allen Wright & Arthur R. Miller, Federal Practice and Procedure § 1364 (1990))
• Raising the quality of healthcare is our goal."
• "The defining feature of an HMO is receipt of a fixed fee for each patient enrolled under the terms of a contract to provide specified health care if needed."
• "[T]he Federal Judiciary would be acting contrary to the congressional policy of allowing HMO organizations if it were to entertain an ERISA fiduciary claim portending wholesale attacks on existing HMOs solely because of their structure, untethered to claims of concrete harm."
• stating that HMO is contractually bound to provide promised benefits, even if the cost of medically necessary treatment exceeds premiums paid
• discussing financial structure of HMOs and the fact that profits are tied to physicians' rationing care
• explaining that the Employee Retirement Income Security Act altered the common law of trusts to permit certain actions that would otherwise violate the trustee’s fiduciary duties
• explaining that the Employee Retirement Income Security Act altered the common law of trusts to permit certain actions that would otherwise violate the trustee’s fiduciary duties
• distinguishing questions of jurisdiction raised after entry of final judgment from uncontested issues related to the propriety of removal
• insurer does not act in a fiduciary capacity under ERISA when it “mak[es] decisions . . . influenced by the terms” of the agreement between the insurer and employer, even when insurer “ultimately profit[s] from [its] own choices to minimize the medical services provided.”
• noting proper inquiry is whether person or entity performed a fiduciary function when taking action subject to complaint
• concluding that "when employers contract with an HMO to provide benefits to employees subject to ERISA, the provisions of documents that set up the HMO are not, as such, an ERISA plan"
• "The defining feature of an HMO is receipt of a fixed fee for each patient enrolled under the terms of a contract to provide specified health care if needed."
• recognizing that the agreement between an HMO and an employer may provide elements of a plan by setting out the rules under which care is provided
• noting that a physician's "professional obligation to provide covered services with a reasonable degree of skill and judgment in the patient's interest" serves as a check on the influence of financial incentives
• holding that there was “jurisdiction regardless of the correctness of the removal” because the “amended complaint alleged ERISA violations, over which the federal courts have jurisdiction”
• explaining that the Employee Retirement Income Security Act altered the common law of trusts to permit certain actions that would otherwise violate the trustee’s fiduciary duties
• "Judicial estoppel generally prevents a party from prevailing in one phase of a case on an argument and then relying on a contradictory argument to prevail in another phase."
• the HMO is not the ERISA plan, but a separate entity that pre-dates the plan, and the manner in which the HMO compensates its doctors is not governed by ERISA
• “At common law, fiduciary duties characteristically attach to decisions about managing assets and distributing property to beneficiaries.”
• stating that courts may use a party’s brief “to clarify allegations in her complaint whose meaning is unclear”
• "Rules governing collection of premiums, definition of benefits, submission of claims, and resolution of disagreements over entitlement to services are the sorts of provisions that constitute a plan."
• “[T]he common law (understood as including what were once the distinct rules of equity) charges fiduciaries with a duty of loyalty[.]”
